claims.text: The baseline material is a high-entropy alloy in which Ti and Ni are primary constituents and each is present at 5–35 at%.
The unspecified additional elements and their concentrations satisfy the stated high-entropy-alloy compositional definition.
The baseline alloy contains no significant refractory-element microalloying.
The intervention introduces 5 at% Mo during melting.
Adding 5 at% Mo can leave the modified alloy within the requirement that every constituent be present at 5–35 at%.
Mo enters solid solution and increases lattice distortion in the Ti- and Ni-primary alloy.
The Mo addition may produce fine Mo-rich precipitates.
The Mo addition may stabilize microstructures at grain boundaries.
Mo-induced lattice distortion, precipitates, or stabilized grain-boundary structures impede dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
Mo increases the activation energy for dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening and possible precipitation effects.
Mo increases resistance to grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed strengthening and stabilization mechanisms reduce the elevated-temperature creep rate.
The proposed strengthening and stabilization mechanisms increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
At approximately 700°C, the 5 at% Mo alloy will have higher yield strength than the otherwise identically processed Mo-free baseline.
At approximately 700°C, the 5 at% Mo alloy will have a lower creep rate or longer creep lifetime than the otherwise identically processed Mo-free baseline.
The magnitude of any improvement may depend on cooling rate, homogenization parameters, and precipitate coarsening at the test temperature.
